pack.title: Engineering Study Tracks
pack.description: Thirty-one reusable lessons with unsolved exercises across algorithms, backend engineering, distributed systems, AI application engineering, forward deployed engineering, and product design. Fixtures are fictional and evidence remains learner-produced.

tracks.description: Recognise nine reusable patterns, explain each invariant, and implement the unsolved Java starters.

tracks.title: Backend engineering
tracks.description: Practise retry-safe APIs, Spring transaction boundaries, and SQL ownership under concurrency.

tracks.title: Distributed systems
tracks.description: Design recoverable work, diagnose overload, and make job creation and claiming safe.

tracks.title: AI application engineering
tracks.description: Put uncertain model output and retried API work behind explicit, testable contracts.

tracks.title: Forward deployed engineering
tracks.description: Follow a discovery-first fictional customer delivery from scoping through productization.

tracks.title: Product design
tracks.description: Frame the operator problem, model recovery states, and build an accessible interface.

sessions.title: Two Sum
sessions.prompt: Given unsorted numbers and a target, return indices of two values that add to the target.
options: Hash map / complement lookup
Sliding window
Topological sort
Union-find
sessions.feedback: Name the property in the prompt that makes a pattern safe. If the input is sorted and you only need the pair, two pointers may avoid the map.
sessions.model: The number you need is determined by the number you see: need = target − current. Store prior values so each new value can ask whether its partner already exists.
sessions.example: nums = [2, 7, 11, 15], target = 9
sessions.trigger: Unsorted array + “pair that equals target” + one pass is possible.
sessions.nonTrigger: If the input is sorted and you only need the pair, two pointers may avoid the map.
sessions.invariant: Before processing index i, the map contains values from earlier indices only.

trace.note: Start with an empty map: value → earlier index.
7 is absent, so record 2 → 0.
2 is present. The earlier index and current index form the pair.

decision.prompt: nums=[3,3], target=6. What must happen before inserting the second 3?
options: Look for its complement among earlier indices
Overwrite the first index
Return the same index twice
decision.feedback: The earlier 3 and the current 3 are distinct indices. Looking up first preserves that distinction.

sessions.title: Two Sum II
sessions.prompt: Given a sorted array and a target, find the two positions that add to it.
options: Prefix sum
Opposing two pointers
Monotonic deque
DFS
sessions.feedback: Name the property in the prompt that makes a pattern safe. Unsorted input has no safe direction to move a pointer without extra structure.
sessions.model: Sorting gives you an order-based elimination rule. A sum that is too small cannot be fixed by moving the right pointer left; move the left pointer right. A sum too large means move the right pointer left.
sessions.trigger: Sorted input + two values + target sum.
sessions.nonTrigger: Unsorted input has no safe direction to move a pointer without extra structure.
sessions.invariant: If a valid pair exists, it remains inside the current [left, right] interval.

trace.note: 2+15 is too large, so discard 15 by moving R left.
Still too large; move R left again.
Match. No pair outside this interval was wrongly discarded.

decision.prompt: Sorted [-4,1,3,8], target=4. The endpoints sum to 4. What did ordering allow?
options: Discard endpoints safely when a sum was too small or large
Use a window even without ordering
Assume every value is positive
decision.feedback: The safe elimination rule comes from sorted order, not positivity.

sessions.title: Subarray Sum Equals K
sessions.prompt: Count continuous subarrays whose sum equals k. Values may be negative.
options: Prefix sum + frequency map
Binary search
Union-find
Stack
sessions.feedback: Name the property in the prompt that makes a pattern safe. A positive-only “at most / exactly” sum question may permit a sliding window instead.
sessions.model: If currentPrefix − oldPrefix = k, the range between those positions sums to k. Count every earlier prefix equal to currentPrefix − k.
sessions.example: nums=[1,1,1], k=2; freq={0→1}, prefix=0
sessions.trigger: “Count subarrays” + sum property + negatives or no monotonicity.
sessions.nonTrigger: A positive-only “at most / exactly” sum question may permit a sliding window instead.
sessions.invariant: The map counts all prefix sums seen before the current position, including prefix sum 0 once before the array.

trace.note: A prefix is the sum up to a boundary. A range is the difference of two boundary sums.

trace.code:
after first 1: prefix=1
earlier boundary 0 → range sum 1
trace.note: The empty prefix allows a range beginning at the first element. It is one earlier boundary.
The same sum occurs at two boundaries. A set would lose how many different ranges can start.

trace.code:
after final 1: prefix=1
compatible earlier boundary sum = 0
trace.note: Both earlier zero boundaries matter. Count the earlier history before adding this boundary.

decision.prompt: For [0,0], k=0, what is the total number of nonempty matching ranges?
decision.feedback: There are two single-element ranges and one two-element range. Frequencies retain repeated prefix sums.

sessions.title: Longest Substring Without Repeating
sessions.prompt: Return the length of the longest substring with no repeated character.
options: Variable sliding window
Prefix sum
Kahn’s topological sort
Kruskal union-find
sessions.feedback: Name the property in the prompt that makes a pattern safe. “Every window of fixed size k” calls for a fixed window, not variable resizing.
sessions.model: A candidate substring is a contiguous window. When the right edge creates a duplicate, move the left edge only far enough to restore uniqueness; never move either edge backward.
sessions.example: s = “abca”; left=0; seen={}
sessions.trigger: Contiguous substring + longest/shortest + a validity rule that can be restored while expanding.
sessions.nonTrigger: “Every window of fixed size k” calls for a fixed window, not variable resizing.
sessions.invariant: The active window contains no repeated character after each repair.

trace.note: Expand right through a, b, c: the window is valid and grows.

trace.code: right=3 is a; prior a at 0
trace.note: Move left to 1, just after the conflicting a.
Uniqueness is restored; record the best length without moving right back.

decision.prompt: For “abba”, last a was at 0 but left is already 2. Where can left move?
options: Back to 1
Stay at 2
Back to 0
decision.feedback: Never move left backward. A last-seen index outside the active window must not reopen invalid history.

sessions.title: Daily Temperatures
sessions.prompt: For each day, find how many days until a warmer temperature.
options: Monotonic stack
Two pointers
BFS
Prefix-sum map
sessions.feedback: Name the property in the prompt that makes a pattern safe. If you need the best element in a moving fixed-size window, use a deque rather than a stack of unresolved answers.
sessions.model: Keep unresolved days in decreasing temperature order. A warmer current day resolves every colder day at the stack top, because this is the first warmer day they have encountered.
sessions.example: temps = [73, 71, 74]; stack=[]
sessions.trigger: “Next greater/smaller element” or “when will this be beaten?”
sessions.nonTrigger: If you need the best element in a moving fixed-size window, use a deque rather than a stack of unresolved answers.
sessions.invariant: The stack holds unresolved indices whose values are monotonic from bottom to top.

trace.note: Push index 0 (73), then index 1 (71): both await a warmer day.
74 resolves 71 first: answer[1]=1. It also resolves 73: answer[0]=2.
74 now awaits a future warmer day.

decision.prompt: For [73,73,74], may the second 73 resolve the first?
options: Yes: it is later
No: warmer means strictly greater
Only if the index is even
decision.feedback: Equal temperature does not satisfy strictly warmer. Both await 74.

sessions.title: Sliding Window Maximum
sessions.prompt: Return the maximum for every window of size k.
options: Monotonic deque
Hash map
Topological sort
Recursion
sessions.feedback: Name the property in the prompt that makes a pattern safe. A variable validity condition uses a standard sliding window; it does not need monotonic candidates.
sessions.model: Keep only candidates that can still become a maximum. A newer larger value makes smaller values behind it permanently useless; expired indices leave from the front.
sessions.example: nums=[1,3,1], k=2; deque=[]
sessions.trigger: Maximum/minimum of every fixed-size window, especially stream-like input.
sessions.nonTrigger: A variable validity condition uses a standard sliding window; it does not need monotonic candidates.
sessions.invariant: Deque indices are inside the window and their values decrease from front to back; the front is the maximum.

trace.note: Read 1: deque=[0]. Read 3: remove 0 because 1 can never beat the newer 3.

trace.code: deque=[1]; first full window ends at 1
trace.note: Front index 1 gives max 3.
Keep 1 behind 3 while both remain in the window. Front stays the max.

decision.prompt: A deque index is left of the current window. What happens?
options: Keep it if its value is large
Expire it before reading the maximum
Sort the entire window
decision.feedback: Candidate value alone is insufficient: an expired index cannot answer this window.

sessions.title: Number of Closed Islands
sessions.prompt: Count land regions completely surrounded by water in a grid.
options: Grid DFS / BFS
Topological sort
Union-find only
Binary search
sessions.feedback: Name the property in the prompt that makes a pattern safe. Prerequisite/order language is a directed-graph cue, not a grid traversal cue.
sessions.model: A grid is a graph: each land cell connects to adjacent land cells. First eliminate every land region touching a boundary; what remains is closed.
sessions.example: Boundary land cell found
sessions.trigger: Grid + connected regions + visit each cell at most once.
sessions.nonTrigger: Prerequisite/order language is a directed-graph cue, not a grid traversal cue.

trace.note: Start a flood fill from it and mark its entire component visited.
It cannot reach a boundary because all boundary-connected land was removed.
Count one closed island and continue scanning.

decision.prompt: One zero-cell path reaches an outer edge. Is that entire connected component closed?
options: Yes if most cells are internal
No
Only if visited with DFS
decision.feedback: Reachability to the boundary is a property of the whole component; traversal order cannot change it.

sessions.title: Is Graph Bipartite?
sessions.prompt: Can graph nodes be split into two groups so every edge crosses groups?

Monotonic stack
Prefix sum

sessions.model: Assign a colour, then every neighbour must be the opposite. A contradiction means an odd cycle prevents a valid split.

options: Yes

Only with a queue of strings

sessions.title: Min Cost to Connect All Points
sessions.prompt: Connect every point with minimum total Manhattan-distance cost.
options: MST / Kruskal + union-find
Sliding window
Topo sort
Recursion only
sessions.feedback: Name the property in the prompt that makes a pattern safe. A single source-to-destination cheapest path is Dijkstra territory, not an MST.
sessions.model: This is “connect everything cheaply,” which is a minimum spanning tree. Sort candidate edges; take an edge only when it joins two previously separate components.
sessions.example: Sort edges by cost
sessions.trigger: Connect all nodes + minimum total cost + cycles add no value.
sessions.nonTrigger: A single source-to-destination cheapest path is Dijkstra territory, not an MST.
sessions.invariant: Chosen edges never create a cycle; the union-find represents the current connected components.

trace.note: Initially every point is its own component.
Different components: take it and union A/B.

trace.code: Consider a later edge within A/B component
trace.note: Skip it: it would form a cycle and cannot help connect a new component.

decision.prompt: An edge joins vertices already in the same union-find set. What do you do in Kruskal?
options: Take it because it is cheap
Skip it: it closes a cycle
Clear the union-find
decision.feedback: A spanning tree connects components without cycles. Consider edges by weight and stop after n−1 accepted edges.

sessions.title: A retry should not create another job
sessions.prompt: A fictional migration operator submits a job. The response is lost, so the client repeats the same request. Which contract prevents a second job?
options: Disable the button for five seconds
Persist an idempotency key, request identity and result together
Retry until an HTTP 200 arrives
sessions.feedback: A browser control cannot prevent a network retry or a second client. Locate the durable boundary.
sessions.model: A retry repeats an intention after an uncertain result. Give that intention an identity. Atomically reserve the key with the job, and replay the original result for the same payload. The same key with a different payload is a conflict. An in-memory map teaches the mechanism; multiple processes require shared durable enforcement.
sessions.example:
key=import-42, payload={tenant:"demo", batch:"B7"}
POST succeeds → response lost → same POST
sessions.trigger: A side effect can be retried after its outcome becomes uncertain.
sessions.nonTrigger: A new intention needs a new key. Similar payloads alone do not mean the same intention.
sessions.invariant: At most one accepted job per scoped key; a key cannot silently change meaning.

trace.note: A separate read followed by an insert has a race. Define what is atomic.
A crash after this commit still leaves a result to replay.

trace.code: request B → same key, same fingerprint
trace.note: Return the recorded job identity. Do not create another side effect.

decision.prompt: Two processes both see “key absent”. What protects correctness?
options: A shared unique constraint and a transaction around creation
A sleep before insertion
A Java HashMap in each process
decision.feedback: Only shared atomic enforcement arbitrates both writers. Also define how an in-progress request is represented.

sessions.title: Where does the transaction begin?
sessions.prompt: A method calls this.createJob(), whose annotation is @Transactional. In default proxy mode, what establishes the transaction?
options: The annotation always runs, including self-invocation
A call through the transactional proxy
The Java compiler inserts a database lock
sessions.feedback: Distinguish an annotation from the mechanism that intercepts a method call.
sessions.model: In default Spring proxy mode, advice runs when a call crosses the proxy. A call on this stays inside the target. Put the boundary where a real caller crosses it, or deliberately choose a different supported mechanism. Rollback rules also matter: an annotation is not a promise that every failure rolls back.
sessions.example:
controller → service proxy → createJob()
service target → this.createJob() bypasses that proxy
sessions.trigger: A transaction annotation exists but a write partly survives a failure.
sessions.nonTrigger: This rule describes default proxy mode; AspectJ weaving is a different mechanism.
sessions.invariant: Job and idempotency record must commit or roll back as one unit at the actual intercepted boundary.

trace.note: The interceptor can begin or join a transaction.
The self-call does not cross the proxy; inspect the outer transaction too.
Check runtime versus checked exceptions and explicit rollback configuration.

decision.prompt: An outer method is already transactional and calls an unadvised inner method. Does that inner work necessarily run without a transaction?
options: Yes, because it bypasses the proxy
No; it can participate in the transaction already active
Only if it is static
decision.feedback: Proxy bypass prevents applying the inner advice; it does not erase a transaction already active on that execution.

sessions.title: Claim a job without claiming it twice
sessions.prompt: Two workers read the same pending row, then each marks it running. What must the design make atomic?
options: Selecting and claiming ownership under a defined concurrency contract
Printing the job ID
Increasing the query timeout
sessions.feedback: A successful read does not reserve a row. Follow the two writers between statements.
sessions.model: A query observes data; a claim changes who may act. Make the transition conditional or lock the row within a short transaction. Define what happens when another worker wins, a lease expires, or a process dies. Isolation levels and database-specific locking behavior are part of the contract.
sessions.example:
worker A: SELECT pending → J7
worker B: SELECT pending → J7
Both now believe they own J7.
sessions.trigger: Read-then-write decisions compete on shared rows.
sessions.nonTrigger: Raising isolation alone does not specify your retry or external side-effect behavior.
sessions.invariant: At most one current owner can transition a job from pending to running; stale owners cannot commit newer work.

trace.code: A reads J7; B reads J7
trace.note: Plain snapshots can overlap. The duplicate claim has not yet been prevented.

trace.code: conditional UPDATE or row lock in a transaction
trace.note: Define a single winner and an observable losing result.
A recovery policy needs a lease or explicit operator action, plus stale-owner protection.

options: It owns the job anyway
The claim did not succeed; it must not perform the side effect
The database is empty
decision.feedback: Check affected-row count or returned rows. A lost race is a real outcome.

sessions.title: Design the migration control plane
sessions.prompt: A fictional operator needs to submit, pause and inspect migration jobs. Legacy traffic must continue. What should the first design step establish?
options: Which queue brand to use
User operations, correctness invariants and failure/rollback requirements
A microservice for every noun
sessions.feedback: Technology choices need a workload and correctness contract to answer to.
sessions.model: Separate the control plane that records intent from workers that perform bounded units of work. Durable job state explains what is accepted, running, retryable or terminal. Evolve through a small compatible slice, instrument it, then expand. A queue can redeliver: state transitions and idempotent effects must make retries safe.
sessions.example:
operator → job API → job state → bounded work queue → worker
                      ↑ progress and reconciliation ←
sessions.trigger: Long-running work needs visibility, bounded concurrency, compatibility and recovery.
sessions.nonTrigger: A diagram with arrows is not evidence that rollback or exactly-once effects work.
sessions.invariant: An accepted job is recoverable; progress reflects durable work; retries cannot corrupt migrated data.

trace.note: Identify the gap between commit and enqueue. Decide how the intent survives a crash.
Name the deduplication boundary at the destination, not only at the queue.
Stop new admissions, preserve diagnostic state, and apply the scoped rollback/repair plan.

decision.prompt: Writes commit but the enqueue call fails. Which design closes the gap without pretending both systems share a transaction?

sessions.title: Retrieve only what the caller may use
sessions.capability: Secure ingestion, document ACLs, permission-filtered RAG, citations and evals
sessions.prompt: The assistant finds a highly relevant document that the Slack user cannot read. Where must the boundary hold?
options: Let the model decide whether to reveal it
Filter and validate permissions before content reaches model context, caches or output
Hide the citation but include the answer
sessions.feedback: A prompt cannot turn unauthorized context into authorized data. Retrieval and cache boundaries need the caller’s current permissions.
sessions.model: Carry source identity, tenant, document version and ACL provenance through ingestion and retrieval. Quarantine unknown ingestion status and stale permissions. Build authorized context before generation, then validate cited references and output against that context. Re-check permissions when serving cached answers. A deterministic fixture suite proves these specified boundary behaviors; retrieval quality, factual support and live-model behavior need separate evaluation.

source + ACL → safe ingestion → tenant/permission filter → context → cited answer
permission changed → invalidate or revalidate index + cache before reuse
sessions.trigger: A Slack assistant combines private CRM facts and documents for users with different permissions.
sessions.nonTrigger: Citation presence is not evidence that an answer is true; a vector match is not an access grant.
sessions.invariant: Unauthorized, revoked, stale-ACL or quarantined content never becomes usable answer context or a served cached answer.

trace.note: Restrict before assembling context. A same-tenant match alone does not grant document access.

trace.note: Revalidate or invalidate. Index metadata can lag the source; freshness is an explicit contract.

trace.note: Reject references outside context and forbidden actions. Human review still checks semantic support.

sessions.title: Recover the service and keep the customer informed
sessions.capability: Production debugging, rollback, postmortems and customer outage communication
sessions.prompt: A fictional release is followed by CRM timeouts and delayed Slack answers. What should the first customer update communicate?
options: The deploy is definitely the root cause
Observed impact, current mitigation or investigation, unknowns and the next update checkpoint
A guaranteed restoration time without evidence
sessions.feedback: The customer needs reliable information and a next checkpoint. A nearby deploy is evidence for a hypothesis, not proof of a cause.
sessions.model: Handle the technical incident and communication as one timeline. Assign command, investigation and communication responsibilities, limit harm, preserve evidence and test competing causes. A rollback has a scope and compatibility condition. Recovery requires the original user task to work again, including backlog and permissions. A postmortem records causal confidence and owned follow-up work rather than blame or retrospective certainty.
sessions.example:
observe impact → declare roles → mitigate → verify customer task → reconcile backlog
customer updates refer to the same timeline
sessions.trigger: A live or simulated failure needs bounded recovery and clear customer expectations.
sessions.nonTrigger: A written incident plan or fictional postmortem is not production incident ownership.
sessions.invariant: Every claimed impact, mitigation and recovery is anchored to an observation; uncertainty remains explicit.

trace.note: Build a timeline and two hypotheses. State which observation distinguishes them.

trace.code: bounded admission or rollback → same measurements
trace.note: Name a decision owner, rollback trigger and data compatibility check; verify whether the intervention helped.

trace.code: answers recover; queued work reconciles; update customer
trace.note: Check duplicate side effects, permissions and delayed work before declaring the incident resolved.

decision.prompt: Latency improves after rollback, but queued jobs still fail. Is the customer incident fully resolved?
options: Yes, the graph is lower
No; verify and reconcile the incomplete customer work before closing
Delete failed jobs to clear the chart
decision.feedback: A partial metric recovery does not restore every affected workflow. Backlog and side-effect correctness belong in verification.

sessions.capability: Adoption, usage, expansion and churn signals, defensible ROI measurement
sessions.prompt: The fictional assistant received more messages this week. Does this establish customer value?
options: Yes, more messages prove ROI
No; connect eligible-user adoption and successful tasks to a baseline, cost and uncertainty
Only if the chart is animated
sessions.feedback: Retries, bots and unsuccessful work can increase volume. Define useful completion and the population before telling a value story.
sessions.model: Turn the discovery acceptance scenario into a measurement contract. Define an eligible cohort, a useful task and a time window, then distinguish activation, repeated use, task success and cost. Compare a compatible baseline and include setup, operation and review effort. A hypothetical ROI calculation explores assumptions; it does not prove causal savings. Expansion or churn signals prompt a customer conversation, not an automatic commercial conclusion.
sessions.example:
eligible people → first useful answer → repeated useful use
value hypothesis = supported task benefit − stated delivery and operating costs
sessions.trigger: A delivery must show whether the original problem improved and what to investigate next.
sessions.nonTrigger: Synthetic activity, time spent and raw request totals are not measured adoption, retained customers or revenue.
sessions.invariant: Every metric exposes its cohort, denominator, window, provenance and uncertainty; unknown benefit stays unknown.

trace.code: discovery goal → useful task + eligible population
trace.note: Specify excluded bots, duplicate events and denied attempts without erasing real service failures.

trace.code: baseline and pilot cohorts → repeated use + success + cost
trace.note: Check comparability, missing observations and changed work mix before attributing improvement.

Treat every answer as one hour saved
decision.feedback: Missing inputs are part of the result. A configurable scenario must remain distinct from an observed benefit.
